claim: Approximately 70% of C. elegans genes undergo trans-splicing where the 5′ end is replaced by a common 22-nucleotide leader RNA (SL1).
source: Nascent RNA transcripts from approximately 70% of C. elegans genes undergo a rapid co-transcriptional processing event in which the 5′ end is replaced by a common 22-nucleotide leader RNA (SL1) through a trans-splicing mechanism (Blumenthal, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Blumenthal, 2012, which provides external evidence for this statement.

claim: Trans-splicing removes information about Pol II initiation from nascent RNAs, making TSSs difficult to identify from accumulated mRNAs.
source: Because trans-splicing removes information about Pol II initiation from nascent RNAs, TSSs have been difficult to identify from accumulated mRNAs (Morton and Blumenthal, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Morton and Blumenthal, 2011, providing external evidence.

claim: C. elegans equalizes X-chromosome gene expression between the sexes by reducing Pol II recruitment to promoters of X-linked genes in XX embryos.
source: We show that C. elegans equalizes X-chromosome-wide gene expression between the sexes by reducing Pol II recruitment to the promoters of X-linked genes in XX embryos via a mechanism that utilizes a chromosome-restructuring complex.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data from GRO-seq and GRO-cap experiments comparing wild-type and dosage-compensation-defective embryos.

claim: A separate regulatory mechanism functions in C. elegans to elevate the intrinsic level of transcription from the X chromosomes of both sexes.
source: We also show that a separate regulatory mechanism functions in C. elegans to elevate the intrinsic level of transcription from the X chromosomes of both sexes, so that after dosage compensation, X chromosomes and the two sets of autosomes have equivalent expression.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data showing equivalent expression levels between X chromosomes and autosomes in wild-type embryos.

claim: Promoter-proximal pausing is rare in C. elegans under normal growth conditions.
source: Our analyses reveal that promoter-proximal pausing is rare, unlike in other metazoans, and promoters are unexpectedly far upstream from the 5′ ends of mature mRNAs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by GRO-seq data showing that very few genes (0.38%) exhibit 5′ pausing in wild-type C. elegans embryos.

claim: Promoters in C. elegans are unexpectedly far upstream from the 5′ ends of mature mRNAs.
source: Our analyses reveal that promoter-proximal pausing is rare, unlike in other metazoans, and promoters are unexpectedly far upstream from the 5′ ends of mature mRNAs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by GRO-cap and GRO-seq data showing that TSSs can be as far as 14 kb upstream of previously annotated 5′ ends.

claim: The DCC binds to both X chromosomes of hermaphrodites to reduce transcription by half.
source: The DCC binds to both X chromosomes of hermaphrodites to reduce transcription by half (Meyer, 2010; Pferdehirt et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Meyer, 2010 and Pferdehirt et al., 2011, providing external evidence.

claim: The DCC shares subunits with condensin, a protein complex required for chromosome compaction, resolution, and segregation.
source: The DCC shares subunits with condensin (Csankovszki et al., 2009; Mets and Meyer, 2009), a protein complex required for the compaction, resolution, and segregation of mitotic and meiotic chromosomes (Wood et al., 2010), suggesting that DCC-dependent changes in chromosome structure facilitate transcription regulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Csankovszki et al., 2009, Mets and Meyer, 2009, and Wood et al., 2010, providing external evidence.

claim: GRO-seq biological replicates for each developmental stage had high statistical correlation throughout the genome (Spearman correlation, ρ > 0.94).
source: The two GRO-seq biological replicates for each stage had high statistical correlation throughout the genome (Spearman correlation, ρ > 0.94) and across gene bodies (Spearman correlation, ρ > 0.98) (Figure 1—figure supplements 1–3 and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quality control measure for the GRO-seq experiments, supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Gene expression levels calculated from GRO-seq data correlated well with expression data from microarrays and RNA-seq experiments.
source: Gene expression levels calculated from GRO-seq data correlated well with expression data from microarrays and RNA-seq experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a validation of the GRO-seq method, supported by comparison with independent expression data.

claim: A TSS was identified for 31.7% (6353 genes) of all C. elegans protein-coding genes from at least one of the three developmental stages examined.
source: In total, a TSS was identified for 31.7% (6353 genes) of all C. elegans protein-coding genes from at least one of the three developmental stages examined (Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is a primary result of the TSS mapping effort, supported by GRO-cap and GRO-seq data.

claim: 77% of TSS calls are for genes shown previously to be trans-spliced.
source: Of our TSS calls, 77% are for genes shown previously to be trans-spliced (Figure 1—source data 2) (Allen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a characterization of the TSS calls, supported by comparison with previous trans-splicing data from Allen et al., 2011.

claim: Outrons can be as long as 14 kb and have a median of 260 bp and mean of 753 bp.
source: We found instead that outrons can be as long as 14 kb and have a median of 260 bp and mean of 753 bp (Figure 1—figure supplement 11B).
evidence: This is a primary finding about the distance between TSSs and trans-splice acceptor sites, supported by analysis of GRO-cap and GRO-seq data.

claim: 59% of outrons are longer than 200 bp, 21% are longer than 1 kb, and 2.3% are longer than 5 kb.
source: Fully 59% of outrons are longer than 200 bp, 21% are longer than 1 kb, and 2.3% are longer than 5 kb (e.g., Figure 1—figure supplement 8A–C).
evidence: This is a characterization of outron lengths, supported by analysis of GRO-cap and GRO-seq data.

claim: 3′ UTRs or polyA signals are rare in outrons of >1 kb in length.
source: From 565 such outrons, only 1.4% had an identified 3′ UTR in the Jan et al. (2011) study, and 0.7% had a 3′ UTR in the Mangone et al. (2010) study. Furthermore, only 3.5% had a polyA site (Mangone et al., 2010).
evidence: This is evidence supporting the interpretation that long outrons represent legitimate transcription units, based on analysis of published 3′ UTR and polyA site data.

claim: Many trans-spliced genes have multiple TSSs.
source: Several other noteworthy features of promoters emerged from this comprehensive mapping of C. elegans transcription units and TSSs. (1) Many trans-spliced genes have multiple TSSs (Figure 3A), suggesting that trans-splicing has removed the selective pressure to form promoters with a single TSS.
evidence: This is a finding about promoter features, supported by GRO-cap data showing multiple TSSs for individual genes.

claim: Trans-splicing has removed the selective pressure to form promoters with a single TSS.
source: Many trans-spliced genes have multiple TSSs (Figure 3A), suggesting that trans-splicing has removed the selective pressure to form promoters with a single TSS.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observation that many trans-spliced genes have multiple TSSs, based on logical inference.

claim: Genes can use different TSSs across developmental stages, indicating developmental stage-specific regulation of transcription initiation.
source: (2) Genes can use different TSSs across developmental stages, indicating developmental stage-specific regulation of transcription initiation (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding about developmental regulation, supported by GRO-cap data showing different primary TSSs for the same gene in different developmental stages.

claim: DNA sequences flanking the newly annotated TSSs have strong sequence conservation across nematode species.
source: (3) DNA sequences flanking the newly annotated TSSs have strong sequence conservation across nematode species (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) and also have evolutionarily conserved core promoter elements, including the TATA-box (worm consensus TATAWAWR) (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplements 1A and 2A,B) and the initiator element (Inr) (worm consensus YCAYTY) (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C), both of which facilitate formation of the Pol II pre-initiation complex (Juven-Gershon and Kadonaga, 2010).
evidence: This is a finding about promoter features, supported by sequence conservation analysis and motif searches around TSSs.

claim: The worm TATA-box consensus sequence is TATAWAWR.
source: DNA sequences flanking the newly annotated TSSs have strong sequence conservation across nematode species (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) and also have evolutionarily conserved core promoter elements, including the TATA-box (worm consensus TATAWAWR) (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplements 1A and 2A,B)
evidence: This is a finding from motif searches around TSSs, supported by MEME analysis of sequences upstream of TSSs.

claim: The worm initiator element (Inr) consensus sequence is YCAYTY.
source: and the initiator element (Inr) (worm consensus YCAYTY) (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C), both of which facilitate formation of the Pol II pre-initiation complex (Juven-Gershon and Kadonaga, 2010).
evidence: This is a finding from motif searches around TSSs, supported by MEME analysis of sequences near TSSs.

claim: Accumulation of Pol II at 3′ ends of genes is abundant in C. elegans.
source: Three prominent features of transcription emerged. Accumulation of Pol II at 3′ ends of genes is abundant (Figure 4A–C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B), as is divergent transcription from promoters lacking upstream divergent genes (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This is a primary finding about transcription features, supported by GRO-seq data showing high 3′ pausing ratios.

claim: Divergent transcription from promoters lacking upstream divergent genes is abundant in C. elegans.
source: Accumulation of Pol II at 3′ ends of genes is abundant (Figure 4A–C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B), as is divergent transcription from promoters lacking upstream divergent genes (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This is a primary finding about transcription features, supported by GRO-seq data showing antisense transcription upstream of TSSs.

claim: 3′ accumulation of Pol II is more extensive in C. elegans than in Drosophila.
source: Pol II 3′ accumulation, likely caused by slow 3′ end formation and RNA processing (Gromak et al., 2006), is positively correlated in C. elegans with the expression level of the gene (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and Figure 4—source data 1) and is more extensive in C. elegans than in Drosophila (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a comparative finding, supported by analysis of 3′ pausing ratios in C. elegans and Drosophila GRO-seq data.

claim: 3′ Pol II accumulation is positively correlated with the expression level of the gene in C. elegans.
source: Pol II 3′ accumulation, likely caused by slow 3′ end formation and RNA processing (Gromak et al., 2006), is positively correlated in C. elegans with the expression level of the gene (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and Figure 4—source data 1)
evidence: This is a finding about 3′ accumulation, supported by correlation analysis of GRO-seq data.

claim: First and middle genes in an operon showed more 3′ accumulation than terminal genes or genes not in operons.
source: First and middle genes showed more 3′ accumulation than terminal genes or genes not in operons (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is a finding about the relationship between operon position and 3′ accumulation, supported by analysis of GRO-seq data for genes in different operon positions.

claim: 3′ pausing is longer at genes with another gene to process just downstream.
source: In other words, 3′ pausing is longer at genes with another gene to process just downstream.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observation that first and middle genes in operons have more 3′ accumulation, based on logical inference.

claim: Upstream divergent transcripts from a promoter without a divergent gene partner are short and initiated 75–150 bp upstream from TSSs.
source: In C. elegans, divergent transcripts are short and initiated 75–150 bp upstream from TSSs of promoters lacking upstream divergent genes (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: This is a finding about divergent transcription, supported by GRO-seq and GRO-cap data showing antisense transcription upstream of TSSs.

claim: The frequency of upstream divergent transcription in C. elegans appears to be intermediate in degree between that in mammals and that in Drosophila.
source: The frequency of upstream divergent transcription in C. elegans appears to be intermediate in degree between that in mammals, where it occurs at the majority of active promoters (Kapranov et al., 2007; Core et al., 2008; Seila et al., 2008), and that in Drosophila, where it occurs only rarely (Nechaev et al., 2010; Core et al., 2012) (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a comparative finding, supported by analysis of sense/antisense transcription ratios in C. elegans, mammals, and Drosophila.

claim: Promoters with TATA elements rarely support divergent transcription in both mammals and worms.
source: For both mammals and worms, promoters with TATA elements rarely support divergent transcription (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D,E) (Core et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a finding about the relationship between TATA elements and divergent transcription, supported by analysis of GRO-seq data for promoters with TATA elements.

claim: Without sdc-2, DCC subunits fail to bind to X, and her-1 is expressed, causing XX embryos to become severely masculinized and die from overexpression of X-chromosome genes.
source: Without sdc-2, DCC subunits fail to bind to X, and her-1 is expressed, causing XX embryos to become severely masculinized and die from overexpression of X-chromosome genes (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a description of the consequences of disrupting sdc-2, supported by established knowledge about the genetic pathway and experimental observations.

claim: her-1 was de-repressed 12.7-fold in sdc-2 mutants.
source: her-1 was de-repressed 12.7-fold, and the increase in GRO-seq signal was uniform from the promoter to the 3′ end, suggesting that SDC-2 controls sex determination by reducing Pol II recruitment or initiation at the her-1 promoter in XX embryos (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from GRO-seq data comparing her-1 expression in sdc-2 mutants vs. control embryos.

claim: The increase in her-1 GRO-seq signal was uniform from the promoter to the 3′ end in sdc-2 mutants, suggesting that SDC-2 controls sex determination by reducing Pol II recruitment or initiation at the her-1 promoter in XX embryos.
source: her-1 was de-repressed 12.7-fold, and the increase in GRO-seq signal was uniform from the promoter to the 3′ end, suggesting that SDC-2 controls sex determination by reducing Pol II recruitment or initiation at the her-1 promoter in XX embryos (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the GRO-seq data for her-1, based on the uniform increase in signal across the gene.

claim: The median change of gene expression in sdc-2 mutant vs control embryos was an increase of 1.63- to 1.67-fold for X-linked genes.
source: The median change of gene expression in sdc-2 mutant vs control embryos was an increase of 1.63- to 1.67-fold for X-linked genes of all lengths and a slight reduction of 0.79- to 0.81-fold for autosome-linked genes (Figure 5—source data 1 and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from GRO-seq data comparing gene expression in sdc-2 mutants vs. control embryos.

claim: The median change of gene expression in sdc-2 mutant vs control embryos was a slight reduction of 0.79- to 0.81-fold for autosome-linked genes.
source: The median change of gene expression in sdc-2 mutant vs control embryos was an increase of 1.63- to 1.67-fold for X-linked genes of all lengths and a slight reduction of 0.79- to 0.81-fold for autosome-linked genes (Figure 5—source data 1 and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from GRO-seq data comparing gene expression in sdc-2 mutants vs. control embryos.

claim: For the subset of X and autosomal genes whose expression was statistically different (p≤0.05) between mutant and control embryos, 99% of X-linked genes had elevated expression in the mutants.
source: For the subset of X and autosomal genes whose expression was statistically different (p≤0.05) between mutant and control embryos, 99% of X-linked genes had elevated expression in the mutants, while 63–66% of autosomal genes had reduced expression (Figure 5—source data 1 and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from GRO-seq data comparing gene expression in sdc-2 mutants vs. control embryos.

claim: For the subset of X and autosomal genes whose expression was statistically different (p≤0.05) between mutant and control embryos, 63–66% of autosomal genes had reduced expression in the mutants.
source: For the subset of X and autosomal genes whose expression was statistically different (p≤0.05) between mutant and control embryos, 99% of X-linked genes had elevated expression in the mutants, while 63–66% of autosomal genes had reduced expression (Figure 5—source data 1 and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from GRO-seq data comparing gene expression in sdc-2 mutants vs. control embryos.

claim: Most embryonically expressed X-linked microRNAs are dosage compensated.
source: We found most embryonically expressed X-linked microRNAs to be dosage compensated (Figure 5D and Figure 5—source data 1, and 'Materials and methods'), while X-linked tRNAs were not, implying that RNA polymerase II is broadly sensitive to dosage compensation, and RNA polymerase III is insensitive (Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding from GRO-seq data comparing microRNA expression in sdc-2 mutants vs. control embryos.

claim: X-linked tRNAs are not dosage compensated, implying that RNA polymerase II is broadly sensitive to dosage compensation, and RNA polymerase III is insensitive.
source: We found most embryonically expressed X-linked microRNAs to be dosage compensated (Figure 5D and Figure 5—source data 1, and 'Materials and methods'), while X-linked tRNAs were not, implying that RNA polymerase II is broadly sensitive to dosage compensation, and RNA polymerase III is insensitive (Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observation that microRNAs (transcribed by Pol II) are dosage compensated while tRNAs (transcribed by Pol III) are not.

claim: The peak of DCC binding is immediately upstream of the TSS.
source: Mapping of new TSSs relative to DCC binding sites called from our ChIP-seq experiments performed for this comparison showed the peak of DCC binding to be immediately upstream of the TSS (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a finding from ChIP-seq data for the DCC subunit DPY-27, analyzed relative to the newly annotated TSSs.

claim: DCC binding to a gene is neither necessary nor sufficient for the compensation of that gene.
source: Although the DCC binds to promoter regions, prior studies showed that DCC binding to a gene is neither necessary nor sufficient for the compensation of that gene, and not all genes are dosage compensated (Jans et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a conclusion from prior studies, supported by citation to Jans et al., 2009.

claim: The DCC can act at a distance to control gene expression, and DCC binding intensity is not a proxy for the dosage compensation status of the gene.
source: Thus, the DCC can act at a distance to control gene expression, and DCC binding intensity is not a proxy for the dosage compensation status of the gene.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the comparison of DCC binding upstream of TSSs to the increase in gene expression caused by disrupting sdc-2.

claim: Very few genes (0.38%, 15 of 3975) of wild-type C. elegans embryos showed evidence of 5′ pausing.
source: In contrast to Drosophila and mammalian genomes, very few genes (0.38%, 15 of 3975) of wild-type C. elegans embryos showed evidence of 5′ pausing (Figure 4—source data 1, Figure 6A,B, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from GRO-seq data analyzing 5′ pausing ratios in wild-type embryos.

claim: The paused genes were not enriched on X in wild-type embryos.
source: The paused genes were not enriched on X (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of the chromosomal distribution of paused genes.

claim: The number of 5′ paused genes was not decreased in sdc-2 mutants.
source: Moreover, the number of 5′ paused genes was not decreased in sdc-2 mutants (Figure 4—source data 1 and Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This is a finding from comparison of 5′ pausing ratios in sdc-2 mutants vs. control embryos.

claim: Genes not paused in embryos become paused in L1s deprived of food.
source: Nonetheless, the GRO-seq assay is capable of detecting 5′ pausing in C. elegans, since genes not paused in embryos become paused in L1s deprived of food (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is a finding from GRO-seq data comparing 5′ pausing in embryos vs. starved L1 larvae.

claim: In starved L1s, 7.7% of genes (166 of 2133) exhibit 5′ pausing, and most were on autosomes.
source: In starved L1s, we found 7.7% of genes (166 of 2133) to exhibit 5′ pausing, and most were on autosomes (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from GRO-seq data analyzing 5′ pausing ratios in starved L1 larvae.

claim: Analysis of GRO-seq data comparing transcriptionally engaged Pol II in control vs dosage-compensation-defective XX embryos revealed a uniform increase in the level of engaged Pol II across the entire length of X-linked genes, from TSSs to 3′ ends, in the sdc-2 mutant.
source: Analysis of GRO-seq data comparing transcriptionally engaged Pol II in control vs dosage-compensation-defective XX embryos revealed a uniform increase in the level of engaged Pol II across the entire length of X-linked genes, from TSSs to 3′ ends, in the sdc-2 mutant.
evidence: This is a primary finding from metagene analysis and analysis of individual genes, supported by GRO-seq data.

claim: For the metagene analysis, the ratio of engaged polymerase in mutant vs control was consistently elevated by at least 1.6-fold across scaled X-linked genes, from TSSs to 3′ ends.
source: For the metagene analysis, the ratio of engaged polymerase in mutant vs control was consistently elevated by at least 1.6-fold across scaled X-linked genes, from TSSs to 3′ ends (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from metagene analysis of GRO-seq data.

claim: Metagene analysis of autosomal genes from the same data sets showed only a slight decrease in engaged Pol II across their lengths.
source: In contrast, metagene analysis of autosomal genes from the same data sets showed only a slight decrease in engaged Pol II across their lengths (Figure 7B), consistent with the slight decrease in autosomal gene expression in mutants (Jans et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a finding from metagene analysis of GRO-seq data for autosomal genes.

claim: The ratios of elongation density indices between control and mutant embryos were not significantly different for genes on X compared to autosomes, indicating that dosage compensation does not preferentially affect Pol II elongation.
source: The ratios of indices between control and mutant embryos were not significantly different for genes on X compared to autosomes, indicating that dosage compensation does not preferentially affect Pol II elongation (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of elongation density indices, supported by GRO-seq data.

claim: Re-analysis of previous genome-wide ChIP-chip analysis of Pol II binding relative to the new TSSs showed an approximately twofold increase in the occupancy of hypo-phosphorylated Pol II at the promoters of X-linked genes in sdc-2 mutant vs control embryos.
source: First, re-analysis of our previous genome-wide ChIP-chip analysis of Pol II binding (Pferdehirt et al., 2011) relative to the new TSSs showed an approximately twofold increase in the occupancy of hypo-phosphorylated Pol II at the promoters of X-linked genes in sdc-2 mutant vs control embryos (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is a finding from re-analysis of ChIP-chip data for hypo-phosphorylated Pol II.

claim: In sdc-2 mutants, the levels of sense and upstream divergent transcription were elevated coordinately at promoters on X lacking upstream divergent genes.
source: Second, in sdc-2 mutants, the levels of sense and upstream divergent transcription were elevated coordinately at promoters on X lacking upstream divergent genes (Figure 7G and Figure 7—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of sense and antisense GRO-seq signal at promoters in sdc-2 mutants vs. control embryos.

claim: At promoters on X lacking upstream divergent genes, the level of hypo-phosphorylated Pol II was also elevated about twofold in mutant vs control embryos, as assayed by ChIP.
source: At those promoters, the level of hypo-phosphorylated Pol II was also elevated about twofold in mutant vs control embryos, as assayed by ChIP (Figure 7—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is a finding from ChIP-chip data for hypo-phosphorylated Pol II at promoters with divergent transcription.

claim: C. elegans dosage compensation controls X-chromosome-wide gene expression predominantly by reducing Pol II recruitment to promoters of hermaphrodites.
source: Our combined experiments demonstrate that C. elegans dosage compensation controls X-chromosome-wide gene expression predominantly by reducing Pol II recruitment to promoters of hermaphrodites.
evidence: This is the primary conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of evidence from GRO-seq, ChIP, and analysis of divergent transcription.

claim: In wild-type C. elegans embryos, X and autosomes have nearly equivalent levels of total gene expression.
source: We show that in wild-type C. elegans embryos, X and autosomes have nearly equivalent levels of total gene expression, and that levels of transcribing Pol II are uniform across X and autosomal genes (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from metagene analysis of GRO-seq data comparing X-linked and autosomal genes in wild-type embryos.

claim: In dosage-compensation-defective mutants, the level of X expression and engaged Pol II exceeds that of autosomes by 1.7-fold, from the TSSs to the 3′ ends.
source: In dosage-compensation-defective mutants, the level of X expression and engaged Pol II exceeds that of autosomes by 1.7-fold, from the TSSs to the 3′ ends (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from metagene analysis of GRO-seq data comparing X-linked and autosomal genes in sdc-2 mutant embryos.

claim: There exists a separate mechanism in C. elegans to elevate the intrinsic rate of transcription from the X chromosomes of both sexes, so that after dosage compensation, X chromosomes and the two sets of autosomes have equivalent expression.
source: These results demonstrate the existence of a separate mechanism in C. elegans to elevate the intrinsic rate of transcription from the X chromosomes of both sexes, so that after dosage compensation, X chromosomes and the two sets of autosomes have equivalent expression.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by the observation that X and autosomes have equivalent expression in wild-type embryos, but X expression exceeds autosomal expression by 1.7-fold in dosage-compensation-defective mutants.

claim: The mechanism to elevate X expression works at the level of controlling Pol II recruitment.
source: Our experiments provide evidence that it, like dosage compensation, works at the level of controlling Pol II recruitment.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the uniform increase in engaged Pol II across X-linked genes in dosage-compensation-defective mutants.

claim: GRO-cap has advantages over TSS mapping strategies that use total accumulated RNA or short-capped (sc) RNA as the starting material.
source: GRO-cap has advantages over TSS mapping strategies that use total accumulated RNA or short-capped (sc) RNA as the starting material.
evidence: This is a claim about the advantages of the GRO-cap method, supported by reasoning about the properties of nascent RNAs.

claim: The use of nascent RNAs without base hydrolysis or size selection, as in GRO-cap, enriches the proportion of 5′ capped RNAs within the starting RNA population.
source: The use of nascent RNAs without base hydrolysis or size selection, as in GRO-cap, enriches the proportion of 5′ capped RNAs within the starting RNA population, reduces the level of false TSS calls from RNAs that are capped post-transcriptionally (Fejes-Toth et al., 2009), and increases the probability of identifying TSSs from promoters that are transcribed at low levels.
evidence: This is a claim about the advantages of the GRO-cap method, supported by reasoning about the properties of nascent RNAs and citation to Fejes-Toth et al., 2009.

claim: The GRO-cap strategy permits reliable assignment of TSSs by pairing TSS calls with uninterrupted GRO-seq signal for transcriptionally engaged Pol II between the GRO-cap TSS and the previously annotated 5′ end.
source: Most importantly, the GRO-cap strategy permits reliable assignment of TSSs by pairing TSS calls with uninterrupted GRO-seq signal for transcriptionally engaged Pol II between the GRO-cap TSS and the previously annotated 5′ end.
evidence: This is a claim about the advantages of the GRO-cap method, supported by the strategy used to validate TSS calls.

claim: Multiple lines of evidence showed that GRO-cap signal combined with continuous GRO-seq signal from WB starts defines true TSSs.
source: Multiple lines of evidence showed that GRO-cap signal combined with continuous GRO-seq signal from WB starts defines true TSSs.
evidence: This is a claim about the validity of the TSS calls, supported by multiple lines of evidence including the rarity of 3′ UTRs and polyA sites in long outrons, continuous ChIP-chip signal for Pol II, and the restricted run-on length.

claim: A recent study using scRNAs to map TSSs set the cutoff for TSS calls to be no greater then 200 bp upstream of the previously annotated 5′ ends, thereby not defining TSSs for a large class of genes.
source: The second report also used scRNAs to map TSSs and set the cutoff for TSS calls to be no greater then 200 bp upstream of the previously annotated 5′ ends, thereby also not defining TSSs for a large class of genes (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a claim about the limitations of a previous study, supported by citation to Chen et al., 2013.

claim: A proportion of the upstream enhancer-like signatures identified by Chen et al. (2013) are TSSs giving rise to full-length transcripts.
source: Based on comparison with our data (e.g., Figure 1—figure supplement 12A,B), we propose that a proportion of the upstream enhancer-like signatures are TSSs giving rise to full-length transcripts.
evidence: This is a proposal based on comparison of the authors' data with data from Chen et al., 2013, supported by examples shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 12.

claim: C. elegans appears to lack NELF, suggesting either that DSIF is sufficient in the infrequent cases of pausing or that the core promoter complex or another not-yet identified negative elongation factor participates.
source: C. elegans appears to lack NELF, suggesting either that DSIF is sufficient in the infrequent cases of pausing or that the core promoter complex (Kwak et al., 2013) or another not-yet identified negative elongation factor participates.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism of 5′ pausing in C. elegans, based on the apparent absence of NELF and the observation of infrequent pausing.

claim: The 3′ accumulation of Pol II has been documented previously in flies and humans using GRO-seq.
source: The 3′ accumulation of Pol II has been documented previously in flies and humans using GRO-seq (Core et al., 2008, 2012).
evidence: This is a claim about previous findings, supported by citations to Core et al., 2008 and 2012.

claim: Pol II 3′ accumulation is likely caused by slow 3′ end formation and RNA processing.
source: Pol II 3′ accumulation is likely caused by slow 3′ end formation and RNA processing (Gromak et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a claim about the mechanism of 3′ accumulation, supported by citation to Gromak et al., 2006.

claim: Cues triggering trans-splicing, particularly operon-specific trans-splicing, appear to facilitate 3′ accumulation and perhaps predispose C. elegans Pol II to greater 3′ pausing genome-wide, whether or not a gene resides in an operon.
source: Cues triggering trans-splicing, particularly operon-specific trans-splicing, appear to facilitate 3′ accumulation and perhaps predispose C. elegans Pol II to greater 3′ pausing genome-wide, whether or not a gene resides in an operon.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism of 3′ accumulation, based on the observation that genes undergoing trans-splicing have greater 3′ accumulation.

claim: Pol II accumulation at 3′ ends does not overlap with U-rich regions at 3′ ends.
source: It should be noted that Pol II accumulation at 3′ ends does not overlap with U-rich regions at 3′ ends. Therefore, the high GRO-seq signal is not due to selective enrichment of U-rich RNAs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of U-richness at 3′ ends, supported by comparison with GRO-seq signal.

claim: In Drosophila melanogaster, dosage compensation is achieved by the male-specific lethal (MSL) complex that binds along the single X chromosome of males to double transcription of X-linked genes.
source: In Drosophila melanogaster, dosage compensation is achieved by the male-specific lethal (MSL) complex that binds along the single X chromosome of males to double transcription of X-linked genes (Gelbart and Kuroda, 2009; Conrad and Akhtar, 2012).
evidence: This is a claim about the mechanism of dosage compensation in Drosophila, supported by citations to Gelbart and Kuroda, 2009 and Conrad and Akhtar, 2012.

claim: The MSL complex was proposed to regulate gene expression by controlling transcription elongation.
source: The MSL complex was proposed to regulate gene expression by controlling transcription elongation (Smith et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a claim about a proposed mechanism, supported by citation to Smith et al., 2001.

claim: The elongation model for fly dosage compensation received recent further support from the discovery that dosage compensation is disrupted by impairing the function of SPT5, a transcription elongation factor that co-localizes with the MSL complex on male X chromosomes and interacts physically with the MSL complex.
source: The elongation model received recent further support from the discovery that dosage compensation is disrupted by impairing the function of SPT5, a transcription elongation factor that co-localizes with the MSL complex on male X chromosomes and interacts physically with the MSL complex (Prabhakaran and Kelley, 2012).
evidence: This is a claim about evidence supporting the elongation model, supported by citation to Prabhakaran and Kelley, 2012.

claim: The weight of evidence strongly favors enhancement of transcription elongation as the primary mechanism of fly dosage compensation.
source: Thus, the weight of evidence strongly favors enhancement of transcription elongation as the primary mechanism of fly dosage compensation.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the mechanism of fly dosage compensation, based on the cited evidence.

claim: In worms, reduction in X-chromosome gene expression is primarily achieved by reducing recruitment of Pol II to promoters, while in flies, elevation in X-chromosome gene expression is primarily achieved by facilitating Pol II transcription elongation.
source: In worms, reduction in X-chromosome gene expression is primarily achieved by reducing recruitment of Pol II to promoters, while in flies, elevation in X-chromosome gene expression is primarily achieved by facilitating Pol II transcription elongation.
evidence: This is a comparative conclusion about the mechanisms of dosage compensation in worms and flies, based on the findings of this study and previous studies in flies.

claim: Multiple solutions have evolved to coordinately control gene expression across an entire chromosome.
source: Multiple solutions have evolved to coordinately control gene expression across an entire chromosome.
evidence: This is a general conclusion about the evolution of dosage compensation mechanisms, based on the observation that worms and flies use different mechanisms.

claim: The bulk of evidence now favors the presence of a mechanism to up-regulate X-chromosome expression in males and females of both C. elegans and mammals.
source: The bulk of evidence now favors the presence of a mechanism to up-regulate X-chromosome expression in males and females of both organisms (Deng et al., 2011, 2013; Jue et al., 2013), and our results provide the most compelling evidence to date for C. elegans.
evidence: This is a claim about the current state of evidence, supported by citations to Deng et al., 2011, 2013 and Jue et al., 2013, and the findings of this study.

claim: A major part of the mechanism to increase X expression in C. elegans is to increase the level of Pol II recruitment to promoters.
source: We found that a major part of the mechanism to increase X expression in C. elegans is to increase the level of Pol II recruitment to promoters, as was shown recently for mammals (Deng et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a conclusion about the mechanism to increase X expression, based on the findings of this study and comparison with mammals.

claim: Condensin II in Drosophila induces axial compaction of interphase chromosomes, globally disrupts inter-chromosomal interactions, and promotes dispersal of peri-centric heterochromatin.
source: Condensin II in Drosophila induces axial compaction of interphase chromosomes, globally disrupts inter-chromosomal interactions, and promotes dispersal of peri-centric heterochromatin (Bauer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a claim about the functions of condensin II, supported by citation to Bauer et al., 2012.

claim: Nematodes carrying mutations that disrupt condensin I display elongated chromosomal axes during meiotic prophase and exhibit chromosome-wide changes in the distribution of double strand breaks and crossovers.
source: Furthermore, nematodes carrying mutations that disrupt condensin I, which shares four subunits with the DCC, display elongated chromosomal axes during meiotic prophase and exhibit chromosome-wide changes in the distribution of double strand breaks and crossovers (Mets and Meyer, 2009), providing strong evidence that DCC subunits control intra-chromosomal structure.
evidence: This is a claim about the functions of condensin I, supported by citation to Mets and Meyer, 2009.
